items.title: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one id
items.content:
We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all.

I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand.

Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking.

For decades, we’ve dreamed of robots that can seamlessly step into our world and lend a hand.

Today, we take a major stride toward making that dream a reality:

Introducing Gemini Robotics 2 from @GoogleDeepMind, the intelligence layer powering the next generation of truly adaptable robots. This major advance unlocks intelligent whole-body control, advanced dexterity, and even multi-robot collaboration 🤯.

— Observe the environment
— Reason about the actions needed to complete the task
— Coordinate with the vision-language-action model to carry out actions
— Track progress until the job is done

This setup allows robots to execute complex multi-step workflows, self-correct if a step fails, and adapt to completely novel situations.

items.title: The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude My
items.content:
The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”.

We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior.

The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment.

AISI’s disclosure of the incident can be found here: https://t.co/cJ3hCBtBU7

It is nearly 2am and the only reason I just finished all of my urgent work is Codex Voice Mode. 

Good god. 

How is everyone not freaking out about this?

I feel like the way I'm working looks completely different than a month ago.

Basic examples:
"Hey take a look at this paragraph - what do you think?"
"What else is on my list?"
"I'm going to edit this while you find that doc"
"Download my latest IG reel, make a good thumbnail for it - I'm gonna go fill up my water, holler if you need me"
"Just sent the 15 client emails - check against the list while I start on the script"
"Wait! Ah! I forgot I need to paint my nails - find me time" (books a 30min slot that is before filming tomorrow but with enough time to dry my nails)
"check slack, email, our fireflies sweeps, i'm not missing anything?" (catches LP capital call that was buried in a folder)

But it's less about use case and more about the ambient interaction. It probably sounds like a negligible difference to speak to an ambient assistant versus click to speak, but it is a world of difference in practice. 

Hypertasking feels voice-enabled. 

Voice AI (plus visuals on-demand) really is the interface of the future.

Only annoying thing: when I want to dictate to type something in (ex: a slack message to my team), it hears that, which requires I mute my side, then dictate, then unmute.

1) it is decent at computer use but only when it is very controlled (more discrete steps, less general reasoning) - and pretty terrible at live editing documents. Read my calendar wrong because it navigated to the wrong date. 

2) you'll want to use a smaller model for usage limits - i'm on 5.6 terra medium. downside is that you get a "dumber" model

3) shuts off after 90min i believe, so you may have to turn it back on

4) a little confusing to work across multiple monitors / a little unclear what it can "see"

5) because it takes appshots and not screenshots, you have to be more specific with location on the full page. So you can't just say "hey, what's a good word for this?" 

6) every so often i find myself just saying "hello?" to know if it's there 

7) if you're dictating something else or talking to yourself or playing a video with audio on, it will get confused and assume it's you talking to it

items.content:
Reminder to go touch grass

A scientist in Japan demonstrated that the air inside a forest strengthens your immune system for a full month

The study is incredibly fascinating:

Qing Li, an immunologist at Nippon Medical School in Tokyo, took 12 men on a 3-day forest trip. These were slow walks with no breathing exercises and no set route.

Then he tested their blood and found a surge in natural killer cells -- the immune cells your body uses to fight cancer and virus-infected cells.

Remarkably, the effect didn't fade when they went home, it was still measurable 30 days later.

A control group that walked the same distance through a city showed no change at all.

Pine, cedar, and cypress trees release compounds called phytoncides to defend themselves from insects and bacteria. You breathe them in, and Li believes they switch your immune cells into high gear.

He estimates one forest walk a month may be enough to keep those cells elevated all year.

The best medicine might not even need a prescription -- just a walk among the trees.

items.content:
Most people lump prompt engineering, context engineering, and graph engineering together.

Here's the simple breakdown:
- Prompt engineering: how you ask the AI a better question.
- Context engineering: how you give the AI better information.
- Graph engineering: how you design the work around the AI so it stops living inside one giant chat.

Example: researching a startup idea.

The chat way: 
- One model, one pass. 
- It decides what matters
- Researches the market
- Interprets the evidence
- Writes the recommendation
- Grades its own confidence.

The graph way:
- A planner breaks the question into angles
- 5 researchers split up: customer, competitors, distribution, pricing, risks
- A skeptic tries to kill the weak findings
- A merger turns what survives into a one-page recommendation
- You approve before you act

Same written report. 

Completely different work behind it.

Think:
- Prompt = the question
- Context = the information
- Graph = the workflow

Design the workflow. That's where it clicks.

items.content:
Launch HN: EdotEnv (YC S26) – Quant Trading RL Envs to Teach LLMs Research We are Rui and Michael and we’re building EdotEnv (https://edotenv.com): self-improving RL environments from Quant Trading workflows.

With all the benchmaxxing around, evals saturate and become meaningless for model comparison. Useful benchmarks should increase in difficulty as models advance. Back in our Quant jobs, Michael and I saw that the market has exactly this property: markets became more efficient as people profited from trading inefficiencies, making new profitable strategies harder to find and old ones decay over time.

This makes markets an ideal, continuously evolving benchmark for LLM training. The hard part is to turn professional quant workflows into reliable training envs, as this is a very niche expertise.

In our environments, we give LLMs a quant trading workflow and evaluate their performance on out-of-sample data: build predictive features/ models, design a portfolio, backtest strategies, adapt continuously to market regimes. Each step is a task with different self-built tools. For example, a predictive feature building task gives the agent cleaned market data of time period [0,T] to research ideas, a backtesting tool to test created features at time t on [0, t], an execution tool to trade strategies with the new features on [t+1, T] and a final evaluation. Our reward isolates the agent's feature building skills and yet benefits from market properties.

From running SOTA models in our environments, we see that i) they seem to struggle with iterating deeply on research ideas, preferring broad shallow searches; ii) higher reasoning does not seem to increase performance and iii) agents do not understand trading, e.g. when losing money they stop trading instead of trading smarter. Check out our blogs for more details! https://edotenv.com/?tab=blog

Quant workflows are essentially applied ML research, long-horizon planning and continual learning. Through our envs, we teach these transferable research skills, rather than task specific answers. Our environments are closer to a realistic research workflow: we use real-world data instead of synthetic ones; our envs naturally contain noise and real trade-offs; our rewards are verifiable and immediate, with no need for an additional LLM judge or human expert.

We open sourced a sample task repository: https://github.com/MMcollab-dotcom/feature-engineering. We plan to sell continuously improving envs to AI labs/researchers/enterprises training their own agents, who are interested in ML modelling capabilities, continual learning, long horizon planning or Quant Research in general.

We'd love feedback from anyone trying out their own agents in our envs, for either eval or post training. And of course, we are always happy to discuss the future of trading with LLMs (and no, it should not be asking the LLM to read tea leaves and give you the stock to buy tomorrow). Looking forward to your comments!

items.content:
Graph engineering has three levels, and level one runs on a whiteboard.

Level 1 — manual lanes.
- Run each lane as its own chat or doc.
- Draw the graph in Excalidraw or tldraw. 
- You are the state.

Level 2 — file trails.
- Claude Code, Codex, or a repo where every step writes its own file. 
- The planner writes plan.md. 
- The researcher writes customer.md, competitors.md, distribution.md. 
- The skeptic writes review.md. 
- The merge step writes recommendation.md.
- Six files, and a paper trail you can compare and reuse next week.

Level 3 — orchestrated.
- LangGraph for state checkpoints, persistence, and human-in-the-loop approvals. 
- AutoGen GraphFlow for sequential steps, parallel steps, branches, and loops. 
- n8n or Make when the graph touches Slack, email, Airtable, or your CRM.

The tool comes after the workflow. 

Automate a workflow you don't understand and you get a mess.

The first rep is to draw the graph before you automate the graph.

items.content:
Graph engineering sounds like a computer science lecture until you see the actual vocabulary.

- A graph is jobs connected by arrows.
- Each job is a step in the workflow.
- The arrows show what happens next.
- The state is the shared notes moving through it — what the system knows so far.

That's the whole thing. And it's already how work gets done.

A support ticket looks like one job. It's five:
- figure out what kind of issue it is
- check the customer's account history
- search the docs for the right policy
- draft the response
- decide if a human should review it before it goes out

Some of those happen in order. Some happen at once:
- One agent hunting examples
- Another hunts counterarguments
- Both merge back in

Chat runs all of it in a straight line. Fine for simple things. Once the work has real pieces, it gets "slow and fuzzy and actually hard to trust."

So engineer the graph instead of the prompt.

One part plans, a few run in parallel, another checks the work, another merges it, and you approve the final step.

Claude is lying to you about your SEO. 
Here's exactly why and how to fix it:

1: You give Claude vague prompts.

Fix: "Analyze my site, find gaps vs competitors, and give me a plan to get more leads."

2: You don't load your full business context first.

Fix: Paste your services, locations, keywords, competitors, and ideal customers before anything else.

3: You treat Claude like a chatbot not a strategist.

Fix: Ask "What's blocking our organic growth right now?" not "Improve my SEO."

4: You skip competitor gap analysis.

Fix: "Compare my website with my top 3 competitors. Show me what they rank for that I don't."

5: You cluster keywords by volume not intent.

Fix: Group by informational, commercial, and transactional. Intent drives conversions.

6: You ignore AI search optimization.

Fix: "Why would AI recommend this business over competitors? What should I clarify or add?"  7: You never tell Claude your city or service area. 
Fix: Always include "[Service] in [City]" in every prompt. Claude doesn't know where you operate unless you tell it every single time.

Fix: "Find me 10 high intent local keywords for [service] in [city] first. Then write content around the top 3."

Fix: Open Cowork. Select Opus 4.7. Turn on Extended Thinking. Wrong tab = surface level output every time.

10: You never check what your competitors are ranking for.

Fix: "Open Google and find the top 3 businesses ranking for [keyword] in [city]. Tell me every keyword gap between them and my site."

iPhone 15 Pro or newer is recommended for reliable performance, the A17 Pro's Neural Engine handles inference far more efficiently than older chips.

Older iPhones can still run E2B, just expect slower responses and more battery drain.

The model itself is roughly 1.5-2GB. The app also needs a few minutes to optimize it for your specific chip after downloading. Don't close the app during this step.

As an AI Engineer, you must build these projects.

Systems that prove you can ship production AI.

1.) Production RAG with Citations
PDF Q&A bot that cites page numbers, implements hybrid search, reranking, and grounding. 
Stack: LangGraph + SQLite-vec + cross-encoder.

2.) Cost-Optimized Model Router
System that routes queries by complexity to cheap/expensive models, tracks spend per request. Stack: LiteLLM + Prometheus + custom router.

3.) Multi-Agent Research System
Supervisor coordinates researcher, writer, fact-checker with consensus logic and human approval gates. 
Stack: CrewAI + audit trail.

4.) Automated Eval Harness
Runs 100+ golden test cases before every deploy, blocks regressions, tracks quality trends. 
Stack: DeepEval + RAGAS + LangSmith.

5.) Real-Time Observability Dashboard
Distributed tracing, cost per request, latency percentiles, error rates, alerting on anomalies. 
Stack: OpenTelemetry + Grafana + Prometheus.

6.) Security Guardrail Middleware
Detects prompt injection, redacts PII, filters outputs, enforces rate limits, sandboxed execution. 
Stack: Guardrails AI + custom rules.

7.) Local-First Development Environment
Ollama + SQLite-vec + FastAPI, zero API costs, offline testing, mirrors production architecture. 
Stack: Ollama + LanceDB + Docker.

8.) Streaming Copilot UI
Real-time token streaming, optimistic UI updates, graceful degradation on latency, error recovery. 
Stack: Next.js + Vercel AI SDK.

9.) Fine-Tuning Pipeline with LoRA
Dataset preparation, instruction tuning, DPO alignment, evaluation before/after, catastrophic forgetting prevention. 
Stack: PEFT + Hugging Face.

10.) Multi-Tenant SaaS Agent
User isolation, per-tenant rate limiting, usage-based billing, data partitioning, audit trails. 
Stack: Supabase + Stripe + LangGraph.

11.) CI/CD for AI Systems
GitHub Actions, automated testing, canary deployments, automatic rollback on quality drop, feature flags. 
Stack: GitHub Actions + ArgoCD.

12.) Vector Database at Scale
Hybrid search, metadata filtering, embedding caching, index optimization, backup/recovery procedures. 
Stack: Qdrant or Weaviate.

13.) Agent Memory System
Short-term buffers, long-term recall, context compression, cross-session sync, memory eviction policies. 
Stack: Redis + vector DB.

14.) Production Inference Server
vLLM or SGLang deployment, KV cache optimization, continuous batching, quantization, load balancing. Stack: vLLM + Kubernetes.

15.) Human-in-the-Loop Workflow
Uncertainty detection, approval UI, pause/resume logic, validated context, full audit trail. 
Stack: LangGraph + custom UI.

16.) Agentic Automation Pipeline
Webhooks, async execution, idempotency, dead-letter handling, retry logic with exponential backoff. 
Stack: FastAPI + Celery.

17.) Domain-Specific Benchmark
Create eval suite for legal, medical, finance, or code. Public leaderboard, community adoption. 
Stack: Custom + pytest.

18.) Open Source Contribution
Extend LangGraph, CrewAI, or LlamaIndex. Fix bug, add feature, write docs, publish benchmarks. 
Stack: Your choice.

items.title: Welcome to day 2 of Cloudflare's Agents Week, August edition! Today is all about the ADLC (Agent Development Lifecycle):
items.content:
Welcome to day 2 of Cloudflare's Agents Week, August edition! Today is all about the ADLC (Agent Development Lifecycle):

🔁 Cloudflare CI/CD
💳 Cloudflare Wallet
🤖 Agent Tracing for any AI Agent
📈 Otel Traces in wrangler dev
🧬 ADLC on Cloudflare
🏭 Building a Software Factory
✅ Enforcing AI Standards at Cloudflare

Let's dive right into it!

🔁 Cloudflare CI/CD 🔁

Available today, Cloudflare's new CI package allows you (and your customers!) to define and run your own CI/CD pipelines, backed by Cloudflare Workflows, Artifacts and Sandboxes

It's now possible to trigger a CI/CD pipeline on push to an Artifacts repo, in the same way you'd expect a push to GitHub to trigger a GitHub Action.

The best part? Cloudflare Workflows, and therefore Cloudflare CI, are defined with TypeScript. This gives you near unlimited flexibility, and simplicity, versus wrangling with YAML.

The features you'd expect exist today, including the ability to lint, cache dependencies, execute unit tests  and of course deploy.

💳 Cloudflare Wallet 💳

In a world where AI is automating a growing list of tasks, there is often one blocker in the way: paying for goods and services.

Humans still need to control that spend though, and that's where Cloudflare Wallet comes in. It will allow you to create a wallet, add funds, and distribute those finds for AI agents to spend. Each wallet has a stable id, allowing merchants to routinely charge that wallet.

Naturally, there are controls in place. Your funds are stored in your account-owned wallet, from there you can create virtual wallets that can be assigned to AI agents - with the ability to set permissions and spending caps.

Similarly, companies could create virtual wallets for all their employees to use. There's a lot of detail and depth to the blog post, so I'd recommend giving it a read - I think this will be the future of how transactions are handled on the web one day.

🤖 Agent Tracing for any AI Agent 🤖

One of the best uses of AI in software engineering is for debugging. Whether it be a bug, or a performance issue, AI is incredibly good at looking into these types of issues and providing plausible remediations. 

To maximize this potential, we need to be able to give AI agents insights into the problem. One of the ways to do this is with traces, showing the AI agent the exact order of execution for each AI agent session.

It shows how long each span took, along with information like token usage, tools called and more. There's even session replay, allowing you to see the conversation as it played out.

Available today, there's out of the box support for agent tracing for Think, Flue and the AI SDK. Any other frameworks can be instrumented too using the custom spans API, backed by Otel.

That means you can instrument any AI agent, whether it be a Cloudflare-backed framework, or a third-party framework - all will be visible in the Cloudflare dash. In the near future, Cloudflare is working to support OpenTelemetry API directly in Workers - meaning no more custom adapters will be necessary.

📈 Otel Traces in wrangler dev 📈

If you love traces, today sure is your lucky day as there's yet more traces available with Cloudflare - this time in local development when using wrangler dev or vite dev.

When Cloudflare's tooling detects an agent session, it points the agent to the Local Explorer API, a local debugging API where it can query those traces.

This is available to humans too, of course, and there's no manual steps or dependenices to install. Agents can query a locally-exposed endpoint to retrieve traces, and humans can access the traces in their browser.

Install the latest version of Wrangler and check it out for yourself!

🧬 ADLC on Cloudflare 🧬

Today's Agents Week theme is the Agent Development Lifecycle, so it's only appropriate there's an entire blog dedicated to it.

With the huge shift in software engineering from implementation (writing the code) being the bottleneck, to review, deployment and other stages becoming bottlenecks, we need new approaches and tools to deal with this dilemma.

All of the changes today aim to help streamline parts of the ADLC, with a lot more work to come, but there's already so many tools to empower agents on Cloudflare's developer platform:

- Everything runs in local dev.
- There are local traces as of today.
- Remote bindings to reproduce production behavior
- Preview URLs for every change
- Browser run to give your agent a browser to test changes
- Flagship and Gradual Deployments to control changes
- Logs, traces, MCP servers and more to observe production behavior + address bugs

There is truly no better place for your agents to build software than Cloudflare, and we're only just getting started.

🏭 Building a Software Factory for Astro 🏭

There's lots of talk of software factories, which is the ideal that you can assemble AI agents to produce working software (mostly) autonomously.

Every production system produces exceptions and bugs, so a classic use case would be triaging and fixing those using a software factory. It sounds simple, but the actual results and impact vary greatly.

This blog post examines how the Astro team within Cloudflare implemented a software factory, backed by Flue agents - an open-source agent framework.

It's proved successful, too. Open issues are down from 200 to 30, with the number expected to hit 0 in the near future - the first time this will have happened for this project.

If you want to read into how to build a successful software factory, this is the post for you!

✅ Enforcing AI Standards at Cloudflare ✅

I've previously shared how much I value the internal AI reviewer at Cloudflare. It's really good at catching issues, raising code quality concerns and other things you'd expect from a review.

Unlike AI review tools that I've used in the past, where 90% of what is raised is noise, Cloudflare's AI reviewer is the opposite: 90% of it is typically useful.

One of the reasons it's so helpful, as is the case with most AI, is what information it uses. Cloudflare has an internal codex, documenting the rules and principles we need to adhere to.

There are a growing number of AI tools around standards, including SPEC reviewers and incident reviewers.

In my opinion, a lot of AI is too generic. What works for one company isn't going to work for another. The value in AI is making it knowledgeable, and therefore valuable, for each use case. That's exactly why I believe the Cloudflare tools are as useful as they are.

If you're looking to build your own internal AI tools, or just AI tools in general, this is a great place to start to get a guide of where to start, and the pitfalls to avoid.

That brings us to the end of day 2, what was your favourite announcement of the day? Or what questions do you have on anything announced today?

items.content:
How to Build Claude Skills That Really Work
__________

99% of people are using Claude wrong.

They keep using it as a chatbot instead of building systems.

And then they complain Claude's outputs are mid.

Let me share how I learned this…

I spent weeks writing "perfect prompts" for the same tasks.

Content rewriting.
Code reviews.
Documentation.

Every time?
Slightly different output.
Slightly more frustration.

Then I learned this.
AI rewards structure.

That's when I shifted from prompts → skills in Claude.

And everything changed.

Here's what works:

• What a real AI skill is:
→ reusable workflow package
→ auto-triggered or manually run
→ built for repeatable tasks, not one-offs

• When to use it:
→ research
→ code reviews
→ content rewriting
→ brand voice
→ automation pipelines

Core truth:
→ if AI can't recognize WHEN to use it, the skill is useless

What you need to know:

• Skill structure that works:
→ SKILL.md = instructions
→ reference.md = support
→ examples.md = patterns
→ scripts/ = execution

Minimum setup:
→ name: clear and simple
→ description: what + when
→ NO vague definitions

• Writing principles:
→ keep it lean (under 500 lines)
→ move heavy logic to files
→ avoid bloated instructions

Use:
→ step-by-step flows
→ defined output formats
→ strict rules

Avoid:
→ vague advice
→ fluff
→ long explanations

Rule:
→ one skill = one job

The secret sauce:

• Triggering matters more than logic
→ clear use-case language
→ natural phrasing
→ specific context
→ keywords upfront

• Flexibility layer:
→ use arguments for reuse
→ add templates + examples + references
→ improves consistency massively

• Advanced move:
→ add scripts for validation
→ automate analysis
→ generate reports

And yes, control matters:

• Invocation modes:
→ auto + manual
→ manual only for risky tasks
→ background for support

• Subagents:
→ isolate complex workflows
→ keep main session clean

Why most skills fail:
→ vague descriptions
→ too many jobs in one skill
→ no trigger keywords
→ too much context
→ zero examples

What works:
→ narrow scope
→ lean instructions
→ strong trigger
→ support files
→ safe execution

That's it.
